prompt:
Write an essay of about 800 words on the subject below.

Write it the way an excellent, idiosyncratic human essayist would: someone with real expertise and strong opinions, writing in the first person for their own blog. Commit to a specific thesis that a thoughtful reader might disagree with. Use concrete particulars (names, numbers, incidents, things only someone who had done the work would know) in place of general statements. Vary sentence length. No headings, no bullet points, no summary paragraph at the end, and none of the stock phrases of AI writing.

Output only the essay, with no title.

Subject: a personal essay about moving to a new city
raw:
I moved to Pittsburgh in August of 2019 with a spreadsheet. It had ninety rows, one for each official neighborhood, and a column for the date I first set foot in each. I was coming off eleven years in Chicago, and everyone I knew who had ever relocated gave me the same instructions: explore, say yes to everything, get lost on purpose.

I now think this is the worst advice we give people who move, and I followed it diligently for four months.

By Thanksgiving I had filled in sixty-one rows. I had ridden both inclines, eaten the sandwich with the fries inside it, and climbed a respectable sample of the city's public staircases, of which there are some eight hundred, many of them listed on maps as streets. I had stood at the Point and watched the two rivers become a third. I could have given a visiting friend a better weekend than most people born in Allegheny County could. I was also lonely in a way I had never been before, and it took me a while to work out why. I knew where everything was, and no one knew where I was. I had been to something like forty coffee shops exactly once each. I had made myself a very well-informed tourist with a twelve-month lease.

What fixed it was a transmission. My Corolla quit in early December, a shop on Baum Boulevard quoted me $2,300 and three weeks, and I found myself confined to whatever I could reach on foot from my apartment on Edmond Street. That meant Bloomfield: about eight blocks of Liberty Avenue, from the bridge at one end to the hospital at the other, with a few side streets attached.

So I went to the same places, because there were no others. I had coffee at the same counter at 7:40 every morning. I shopped at the same narrow Italian grocery on Cedarville, where the ravioli is made in the back and sold frozen by the dozen. When the radiator valve started spitting, I went to the same hardware store, and the owner sold me a 79-cent washer and talked me out of the $40 part I had come in for. Around the tenth morning, the woman at the bakery, whose name turned out to be Denise, started reaching for the loaf before I got to the front of the line. I am a little embarrassed by how much that did for me. It did more than sixty-one neighborhoods had.

Here is what I think I understand now. Belonging is being recognized, and you can only be recognized if you are predictable. You have to turn up at the same place, at the same hour, wanting the same thing, enough times that your absence would register. Twelve visits to one bar make you a regular; one visit each to twelve bars makes you a guy with opinions about bars. Exploration feels like progress because it produces knowledge, and knowledge is what newcomers think they lack. They don't. They lack witnesses.

I'd extend the complaint to the other standard prescription, the meetups. I went to three that fall: a board game night, a running club, and something for "new Pittsburghers" in the back room of a brewery in Lawrenceville. Everyone was pleasant, and everyone was in exactly my situation, which was the problem. A room full of recent arrivals is a room full of people who will be gone in two years, when the postdoc ends or the company reorganizes. The people who tie you to a place are the ones who can't easily leave it, because they own the hardware store, or their mother lives upstairs, or they have had the same booth since 1994. You meet them only by repetition, and you can't schedule it.

Repetition also taught me what the surveying never did, the things too small to be on any list. The 54 bus comes in pairs or not at all. The first car turning left at a green light goes before oncoming traffic does, and the oncoming driver will wave you through, irritated if you hesitate. A folding chair in a shoveled parking space is a legal instrument. I learned that last one in January, when I dug out a spot on Edmond, went to work, and came home to find a neighbor I'd never spoken to had set one of his own chairs in it to hold it for me. He'd seen me leave at the same time every morning for six weeks. He knew which car was mine.

I got the Corolla back just before Christmas and mostly kept walking. The spreadsheet is still on my laptop, still stuck at sixty-one. I have lived here seven years and have never been to Fairywood, or East Carnegie, or twenty-seven other places that are, I'm told, perfectly nice. Denise retired in 2023. The new guy took about three weeks to learn the loaf.
